newsitem.title: UK: Euro mutual funds swelled in '96 - JP Morgan report.
newsitem.headline: Euro mutual funds swelled in '96 - JP Morgan report.

text.p: European mutual funds attracted record inflows in 1996, mostly directed at bond funds, with Italy seeing the greatest gains and France the least, according to a report on global fund flows by J.P. Morgan.

Strategists Caroline Meroz and Gary Dugan said net new investment for Europe excluding the U.K. was $136.8 billion and $152.3 billion including the U.K. France lost $17.3 billion, the only country to suffer net redemptions.

Most of the flows underlined continental Europe's preference for bond holdings, with total outflows from equity funds for Europe-ex-UK at $1.2 billion. The UK alone took an additional net $411.6 billion in subscriptions to equity funds.

Domestic equity mutual funds in Italy and Spain continued to attract new investment, with net subscriptions to Italian shares in the black for the second consecutive month and at their highest level since January 1995.

French SICAV assets remained almost unchanged as net redemptions offset the impact of the market's performance. Germany now has the largest mutual fund industry in Europe, followed by Luxembourg and then one-time leader France.
"In aggregate, the major European countries we follow have mutual fund assets of $1.716 trillion, which corresponds to about 65 percent of US mutual fund assets."

J.P. Morgan said Swedish mutual funds had net redemptions in December 1996 for the first time in 18 months, but noted the figure was distorted by heavy profit-taking ahead of changes in capital gains tax for National Savings Funds.
In November, German mutual funds fought off competition from the Deutsche Telekom public offering, recording net inflows of over 1.0 billion marks.
The rise of the US mutual funds market was well documented through the year. J.P. Morgan said 1996 ended with record net inflow of $38.4 billion.
Domestic equity funds took $24.4 billion, a 72 percent increase on the previous month, while international funds (investing outside the US), registered $2.9 billion of fresh money coming in.
J.P. Morgan noted that fund inflows had different impacts in different markets. "Relatively small net inflows into Spanish equities led to a doubling of assets within that catergory."
